--- title: "Testing the robustness of a published claim: the EU-frames case" author: "Pair: [names]" date: today format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 2 code-fold: false df-print: paged execute: message: false warning: false knitr: opts_chunk: fig-width: 8 fig-height: 5 --- ## The claim, and what we are doing to it The original author (OA) studied how citizens frame the European Union. One claim from their paper is our target: > "… poor economic performances … decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (Teney 2016: 619) Operationalised the way the Multi100 project constrained it for its five analysts: does a country's **unemployment rate** (poor economic performance) lower the **cosmopolitan** dimension of EU framing (peace, democracy, free movement, cultural diversity, a stronger say in the world)? The published anchor result was a coefficient of −0.0034, t = −4.03. You hold the data, the tools, and the workflow the project used – and the code you work through is the coordinator's own submitted analysis. You are analyst no. 6, and the question is: how robust is that number to *justifiable* alternative choices? Work through the five tasks below in order, from a setup check to two dots on the live class chart – one explored, one declared. ::: callout-tip ## How the tasks work Every task is a callout box with instructions, a **TODO** you complete, and code chunks that **already run** – so the report renders from the first preview. You edit the prose blanks and, in Tasks 4 and 5, the code. The browser version of this same exercise is on the workshop site if you would rather not install anything; this workspace is the full IDE pipeline. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 1 – Set up, and fix the vocabulary"} **First, the setup check.** If this report renders at all, your workspace is working: the packages are installed, the data are in place, and the helpers are loaded. Render it once now, before anything else. If it does not render, run `source("R/check_setup.R")` in the console – it names the packages you are missing and how to install them. **Then, before touching data, fix the vocabulary.** In the four scenarios below, three are doing one of our three R's, while one is doing something else entirely. **TODO: read the four scenarios and fill in the gaps.** ***Scenario 1:*** A reviewer reruns the authors' Stata `.do` file on the authors' data and gets a *different* coefficient from the one printed in the paper. This is an example of \_\_\_\_\_\_, even though what they *tried* to do failed. ***Scenario 2:*** The analyst uses the authors' submitted replication dataset, but they re-implement the model in R instead of Stata and centre the predictor. Is this a case of \_\_\_\_\_\_ or \_\_\_\_\_\_? ***Scenario 3:*** A preregistered team tests the identical hypothesis on a *separate, much larger* dataset chosen to be theoretically equivalent, and gets results that contradict the original. Their conclusion is that the original analysis has failed to \_\_\_\_\_\_. ***Scenario 4:*** Instead of the survey data used by the original authors, another researcher tests the same underlying idea on social-media texts using a machine-learning classifier method that the original never used. To their surprise, the authors' original findings prove \_\_\_\_\_\_ and the researcher concludes that they provide a reliable middle-range theory of the phenomenon they investigate. *(Answers: 1 reproducibility – the activity is reproducibility even though it failed to match, so the verdict is 'not reproduced'; 2 arguably still reproducibility, a grey area – re-implementing on the same data in different software is a re-computation, though centring the predictor and differing estimator implementations nudge towards robustness; 3 replicability – same question, independent new data; 4 generalisability – the impostor, new data and a new method at once.)* ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 2 – Meet the panel"} The **EU-frames dataset** (`EUframes_cy.csv`) is the country-year panel behind the whole exercise. It is already loaded as `euframes` in the setup chunk, and the copy in `data/` is byte-identical to the one published in the analyst's fork on OSF (osf.io/6zqct – "Multi100 \| Teney_EurSocioRev_2016 \| Analyst_C6HJR", main folder); the official Multi100 archival record is at osf.io/8rtwe. **TODO:** run the chunks, then read the small-multiples figure. Which countries trend down over 2004–2013? Note one in a comment. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # How many countries, how many years, how big is the panel? euframes |> summarise( countries = n_distinct(cntry), years = n_distinct(year), rows = n() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: You should see **27 countries**, **10 years** (2004–2013), and **270 rows**. The outcome we care about first is `mcosmo` – the mean cosmopolitan framing of the EU in each country-year (a 0–1 scale). The predictor is `unemp`, the annual unemployment rate; `growth` is annual GDP growth, and `n_cy` counts the survey respondents behind each row. Every column is described in `data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(euframes, aes(x = year, y = mcosmo)) + geom_line(colour = "grey55") + geom_point(size = 0.7) + facet_wrap(~ cntry, ncol = 6) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2004, 2008, 2013)) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean cosmopolitan framing (0–1)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Mean cosmopolitan EU framing over time, by country – an echo of OA's Figure 1.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cosmo-trend-1.png){#fig-cosmo-trend width=864} ::: ::: Most countries drift gently; a few move sharply around the 2009 crisis. That variation – within a country, over time – is exactly what the fixed-effects model in Task 3 uses. *Practising the OSF pull (optional).* `R/get_data.R` fetches this file from the analyst's OSF fork the way a researcher would, with a workshop-site mirror as a fallback. It is not needed – the file already ships in `data/` – but running it proves you can pull a real published artefact: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Optional: confirm data/EUframes_cy.csv from OSF (uses the local copy offline). source("R/get_data.R") ``` ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 2, continued – name the estimand, draw the graph"} Before estimating, say *precisely* what you are estimating. An estimand has two parts: a **unit-specific quantity** and a **target population** (Lundberg et al. 2021). State it outside any model. **TODO – complete the estimand sentence:** > Unit-specific quantity: the change in \[\_\_\_\_\] for a one-point difference in \[\_\_\_\_\]. Target population: \[\_\_\_\_\]. *(A defensible filling: the change in mean cosmopolitan framing within a country-year, for a one-percentage-point difference in that country's unemployment rate; across EU member states, 2004–2013.)* Now the identification assumptions. `R/dag_starter.R` builds the graph with `dagify()`, where every arrow is an ordinary R formula written the way you read a regression, effect on the left of the tilde and cause on the right. `framing ~ unemployment` is therefore the arrow unemployment → framing. The causal path and the two confounder pairs are switched on; the arguable arrows sit in the same call behind a `#`, each with a line of justification above it. Open the file, take the `#` off any arrow you believe, re-source, and re-run `adjustmentSets()`. A node joins the picture only once some arrow mentions it, so what you see is the graph you have committed to. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} source("R/dag_starter.R") plot_dag(dag) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The starter DAG: unemployment → framing, with country and year as confounders.](index_files/figure-html/dag-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # What must we adjust for to identify the unemployment -> framing effect? dagitty::adjustmentSets(dag, exposure = "unemployment", outcome = "framing") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` { country, year } ``` ::: ::: The starter graph returns `{ country, year }` – exactly what the two-way fixed effects you fit in Task 3 absorb: country fixed effects adjust for `country`, year fixed effects adjust for `year`. The DAG and the model encode the same identification claim. **TODO – answer two questions in a sentence each:** 1. What do **country** and **year** fixed effects adjust for, in plain terms? *(country-constant traits, and shocks common to all countries in a year)* 2. What can they **not** fix? *(a time-varying, country-level confounder – e.g. GDP growth moving both unemployment and framing within a country over time)* Whatever set your DAG returns becomes field 4 of the preregistration you write in Task 5. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 3 – Reproduce the recorded result"} This is the **reproducibility** check. Fit the two-way fixed-effects model the Multi100 Task-2 constraints point to: cosmopolitan framing on grand-mean-centred unemployment, with country and year fixed effects. The target is **t = −3.804** (df = 233, N = 270) – the value on record for analyst C6HJR in the Multi100 dataset. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Grand-mean centre unemployment, exactly as the submitted analysis did. With # two-way fixed effects this shifts the intercept, not the slope or the t – it # is the transformation the constrained specification names, so do it explicitly. euframes <- euframes |> mutate(unemp_c = unemp - mean(unemp, na.rm = TRUE)) # fixest::feols – the bar separates the regression from the fixed effects. m1 <- feols(mcosmo ~ unemp_c | cntry + year, data = euframes) tidy(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-corrected .cell tbl-cap='The constrained model on EUframes_cy.csv.'} ```{.r .cell-code} modelsummary( list("two-way FE (fixest)" = m1), estimate = "{estimate}", statistic = "t = {statistic}", gof_map = c("nobs", "r.squared"), coef_rename = c("unemp_c" = "Unemployment (centred)") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
two-way FE (fixest)
Unemployment (centred) -0.003
t = -3.804
Num.Obs. 270
R2 0.754
``` ::: ::: The coefficient is **−0.00347** with **t = −3.804** – exactly the value recorded for analyst C6HJR, reproduced from the published data and the published model. `feols` reports classical (IID) standard errors by default when two fixed-effect dimensions are present, which is why it matches the `plm` value the analyst used to three decimals. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Everyone gets the same number. So why did five analysts disagree?"} You reproduced the recorded value exactly, and so did everyone else in the room – because everyone ran the same code on the same file. Reproducibility is the cheap R. The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own code for the same claim, and came back with five different answers, one of them not significant. Their pipelines are competent, well-organised work, so the spread is not a quality problem. It is what happens when a claim stated in words leaves several genuinely defensible quantities on the table, and different analysts estimate different ones without noticing they have chosen. Task 2 named the quantity you are after and drew the graph your adjustment set follows from. Task 4 now shows you how far the answer moves when the other choices move. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 4 – Work the menu"} This task is **exploration, and it is meant to be**. Try several specifications, see what each one does, and get a feel for which choices move the estimate and which barely touch it. Nothing here commits you to anything; that is Task 5. `try_spec()` takes one argument per axis of the specification menu, and every argument already carries the baseline you just reproduced – so changing one thing means changing one argument, and everything you do not name stays at baseline. Every call is a real fit on `euframes`. **TODO:** run the four calls below, then write your own. Three or four of your own is plenty. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec() # the baseline itself ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none | gaussian b = -0.00347 se = 0.00091 t = -3.804 on 233 df p < 0.001 claim-aligned partial r = -0.242 (below zero supports the claim) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(outcome = "mpos") # all positive framings, not cosmopolitan alone ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mpos ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none | gaussian b = -0.00485 se = 0.00097 t = -4.986 on 233 df p < 0.001 claim-aligned partial r = -0.311 (below zero supports the claim) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(estimator = "pooled_cl") # no between-country comparison absorbed ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | pooled_cl | all | w:none | gaussian b = -0.00110 se = 0.00220 t = -0.500 on 268 df p = 0.618 claim-aligned partial r = -0.031 (below zero supports the claim) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(sample = "no_bailout") # drop the assistance-programme countries ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | no_bailout | w:none | gaussian b = -0.00042 se = 0.00123 t = -0.343 on 207 df p = 0.732 claim-aligned partial r = -0.024 (below zero supports the claim) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} try_spec(weights = "n_cy") # weight cells by the respondents behind them ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:n_cy | gaussian b = -0.00263 se = 0.00087 t = -3.040 on 233 df p = 0.003 claim-aligned partial r = -0.195 (below zero supports the claim) ``` ::: ::: Everything you try is logged. Print the log to see the small multiverse you have just built – only the axes you actually varied are shown, so the contrast is readable: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_experiments() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Specifications you have tried (5): outcome estimator sample weights b t r_aligned sig mcosmo fe_twoway all none -0.003470 -3.80 -0.242 TRUE mpos fe_twoway all none -0.004850 -4.99 -0.311 TRUE mcosmo pooled_cl all none -0.001100 -0.50 -0.031 FALSE mcosmo fe_twoway no_bailout none -0.000423 -0.34 -0.024 FALSE mcosmo fe_twoway all n_cy -0.002630 -3.04 -0.195 TRUE Spread of claim-aligned r: -0.311 to -0.024 | significant: 3 of 5 ``` ::: ::: When you have tried three or four, decide which one you would defend if you had to, run it once more so it is the most recent, and submit it. It lands on the live class chart as an **exploratory** result: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} submit_exploration() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why label it 'exploratory'?"} Because that is what it is, and the label costs nothing. You chose this specification after seeing what several of them do, so it cannot carry the guarantee a declared choice carries – it might have been chosen *because* of its result, and neither you nor anyone else can now rule that out. Almost no published paper tells you which of its analyses were explored and which were planned. Today's chart does, because the room submits twice: once here, and once in Task 5 after declaring. Watching the two clouds side by side is the point. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 5 – My preregistration"} The point of preregistration is that you commit to a choice **before** you see what it does. It stops you quietly picking the specification that happens to give the answer you wanted. Here the commitment is real in a mechanical sense too: the choices you declare in the cell below are remembered by the session, and every later cell reads them from here – the model builder refuses code that deviates from them. Make one choice on each axis of the specification menu – every axis is live, including the outcome **family** and the **predictor** – then run the cell. `claim_align <- TRUE` is the day's convention, applied automatically: negative framings are reverse-coded (1 − y) and growth's claim-expected sign is flipped, so 'supports the claim' reads as a negative sign for everyone. Multi100's Task 2 fixed unemployment as the measure on a gaussian scale; this menu opens both. That is not a stretch beyond the project – Task 1 of Multi100 already shows three of the five analysts reaching for GDP-growth measures when the choice was theirs. ::: ::: {.callout-important title="How this block maps to a real preregistration"} *A real preregistration, shortened. Each numbered comment maps to a question in the OSF "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org" (the eight-question short form). Because you are reanalysing data that already exist, field 2 also stands in for the prior-knowledge section of the secondary-data template (van den Akker et al. 2021) – the part AsPredicted leaves out.* ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # ============================================================================ # MY PREREGISTRATION – one specification, declared before seeing its result # ============================================================================ # 1. The claim I am testing: ................................................. # 2. The data + what I already know: EUframes_cy.csv (270 country-years, # public); I know the constrained baseline gives t = -3.804. # 3. My one specification – one choice on each axis: my_outcome <- "mcosmo" # mcosmo | mutil | mpos (positive framings) # mcomm | mlib | mneg (negative framings) my_family <- "gaussian" # gaussian | beta (logit-link on the cell # means; beta reports z) my_predictor <- "unemp" # unemp | growth (the claim-carrying measure) my_pred_form <- "raw" # raw | log (growth: raw only; centring or # z-scaling would leave t, r and p # unchanged - not separate analyses) my_copredictor <- "none" # none | growth (beside unemp) | unemp (beside growth) my_estimator <- "fe_twoway" # fe_twoway | fe_country | re | pooled_cl my_sample <- "all" # all | y2004_2008 | y2009_2013 | no_bailout | no_GR_ES my_weights <- "none" # none | n_cy (re is never weighted) claim_align <- TRUE # the day's convention, applied automatically # 4. Why these controls, in one DAG-grounded sentence: ....................... # 5. Supported if the claim-aligned coefficient is negative and p < .05; # undermined if non-significant or positive. I will report what I get. prereg() # checks every choice against the menu and records the declaration ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DECLARED – one specification, recorded before seeing its result: outcome : mcosmo family : gaussian predictor : unemp (raw) copredictor: none estimator : two-way fixed effects (country + year) sample : all weights: none claim_align: TRUE These choices are now fixed for the rest of the session – the later cells read them from here. This rendered cell is your preregistration record: it timestamps the choice before you see its result. ``` ::: ::: An optional mirror form may be used to log preregistrations for the room – the link is shared in the session. It is not required: the cell above, rendered into this report, is your official preregistration. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Task 5, continued – build, run and report"} This is the **robustness** check, and it is the part your classmates cannot copy from you: together the room samples the multiverse of defensible analyses. You have declared your specification; now translate it into model syntax yourself. Fill the outcome, the right-hand side, and the estimator code exactly as you preregistered them. `build_model()` knows your declaration and will not accept anything else; its error messages tell you what is off. Write the log form as `log(unemp)`, and add any co-predictor with `+`. You do **not** write the fixed-effects, clustering, or family syntax here – the estimator and family codes stand for it, and `run_spec()` expands them into the real fit. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_model <- build_model(mcosmo ~ unemp, estimator = "fe_twoway") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model accepted – it matches your preregistration exactly: mcosmo ~ unemp, estimated by two-way fixed effects (country + year) Run it with run_spec(my_model). ``` ::: ::: When the model is accepted, run it. `run_spec()` fits your preregistered specification for real – the estimator, family, sample and weights all expand into the matching `fixest`, `plm`, `betareg` or `glmmTMB` call – and prints its claim-aligned result: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} run_spec(my_model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Your preregistered specification, fitted: mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none | gaussian b = -0.00347 se = 0.00091 t = -3.804 on 233 df p < 0.001 claim-aligned partial r = -0.242 (below zero supports the claim) ``` ::: ::: Read the output like an analyst: the coefficient and its claim-aligned partial *r* (below zero supports the claim). The five Multi100 analysts run from about the 16th percentile of the specification curve (the most strongly claim-supporting) to about the 68th (near the null); your result is about to join theirs on the class chart. Now send it to the room. There is nothing to fill in and nothing to transcribe – `report_result()` refits your declared specification, builds the spec label, and always submits on the claim-aligned scale the chart is drawn on. It prints your submission line and a pre-filled form link; open it and press **Send**. Your dot joins the live [Multiverse](https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication/results.html) chart within seconds, this time labelled **declared** rather than exploratory. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report_result() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Your declared submission (claim-aligned, straight from your preregistration): spec: declared: mcosmo ~ unemp(raw) | fe_twoway | all | w:none | gaussian b = -0.00347 | se = 0.00091 | t = -3.804 | df = 233 | n = 270 | r = -0.242 Open the link below (or copy the URL) – the form opens with every field pre-filled; just press Send. https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSezoAEOnZUfP4pkfN28_XtEBwSyc2RLsXB-h8RPSegF7_t76A/viewform?usp=pp_url&entry.832496914=declared%3A%20mcosmo%20~%20unemp%28raw%29%20%7C%20fe_twoway%20%7C%20all%20%7C%20w%3Anone%20%7C%20gaussian&entry.1656311800=-0.00347&entry.1337458262=0.00091&entry.1940779437=-3.804&entry.1682711955=233&entry.1586392724=270&entry.1660273001=-0.242 ``` ::: ::: If the form will not open on your machine, read the printed numbers to the facilitator and your dot still lands. **A second declared specification?** Edit the preregistration cell, rerun `prereg()`, rebuild, rerun. The mechanics allow it, and the label does not change – so be clear with yourself about what the second one is. Your first declaration was made without knowing its result; anything after it was not, which puts it back in the same category as Task 4. Saying which is which, out loud, is the entire discipline the day is about. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.callout-note title="Taking it home"} You did the whole analysis in a plain folder, with no version control and nothing to sign in to. Putting your own work under version control and publishing the rendered report to a live URL is the natural next step – a git and GitHub self-study module walks it click by click on the workshop site: [Git and GitHub self-study](https://codemoreh.github.io/applied-replication/companion/git-github.html). The `.github/` and `.devcontainer/` folders already in this workspace are what make that path work once the folder is a repository again. ::: ::: {.callout-note title="Going further (optional)"} Time to spare? Each of these is a real fit you can run in this workspace. - **Sweep a whole axis.** `for (e in c("fe_twoway", "fe_country", "re", "pooled_cl")) try_spec(estimator = e)` fits all four estimators in one go, and `my_experiments()` then prints them side by side. The same trick works for any axis on the menu. - **The mirror-image expectation.** The claim is about *positive* framing. Preregister a **negative** dimension instead (`mneg`, or communitarian `mcomm`): if poor economic performance lowers positive framing, does it *raise* negative framing? With `claim_align <- TRUE` the reverse-coding (1 − y) is applied for you, so the result restates itself on the same scale as the rest of the curve. - **Beyond unemployment.** Preregister `my_predictor <- "growth"` (GDP growth, the claim carrier for three of the five original analysts): the claim now expects a *positive* growth coefficient on the positive framings, and the sign convention flips once more automatically. The growth mirror of the Task-3 anchor (`mpos ~ growth + unemp`, two-way FE) gives b = +0.00167, t = 1.59 – non-significant. - **The full SCORE dossier.** OA's paper went through all three Rs in the SCORE programme and got three different verdicts: its push-button reproduction **failed** (the author-provided Stata code referenced file names that did not match what was available), and its preregistered secondary-data replication returned a **sign flip** (a positive coefficient, b = 0.002, p = .046, in the opposite direction to the original). Explore reproduction, robustness, and replication side by side at . ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## References Teney, C. (2016). Does the EU economic crisis undermine subjective Europeanization? Assessing the dynamics of citizens' EU framing between 2004 and 2013. *European Sociological Review*, 32(5), 619–633. Lundberg, I., Johnson, R., & Stewart, B. M. (2021). What is your estimand? Defining the target quantity connects statistical evidence to theory. *American Sociological Review*, 86(3), 532–565. van den Akker, O., Weston, S., Campbell, L., et al. (2021). Preregistration of secondary data analysis: A template and tutorial. *Meta-Psychology*, 5, 2625. Aczel, B., Szaszi, B., Clelland, H. T., et al. (2026). Investigating the analytical robustness of the social and behavioural sciences (Multi100). *Nature*, 652(8108), 135–142.
